On a Samsung, here are your options depending on what you want:

- If you just want to stop using mobile data (but still allow calls and texts):
  - Swipe down twice from the top to open Quick Settings, tap “Mobile data” to turn it off (icon grays out).
  - Or go to Settings > Connections > Data usage > toggle off “Mobile data.”

- If you want to stop all cellular activity (no calls, texts, or data) temporarily:
  - Turn on Airplane mode: swipe down twice > tap “Airplane mode.” You can then turn Wi‑Fi back on if you still want internet.
  - Or disable your SIM: Settings > Connections > SIM manager > toggle off your SIM. This won’t affect your plan; it just disables the line on the phone.

- “No data, but keep calls/texts”
- “No cellular at all”

Also, would you like me to re-enable the cellular connection I turned off earlier, or keep it off for now?

Yes—that’s perfectly okay.

Right now your phone’s cellular connection is turned off, so it won’t make or receive calls or texts, and it won’t use mobile data. Your plan isn’t canceled or changed; this is just a temporary device setting. You can still use Wi‑Fi for internet.

If you want to make sure absolutely no cellular radio is used:

- Tell me and I can re-enable it for you, or
- On your Samsung: Settings > Connections > SIM manager > toggle your SIM back on, or just turn off Airplane mode if you used that.

I checked the network, and it’s reporting normal right now—no widespread outages on our side.

Let’s pin down what’s “weird.” A few quick questions:

- When did it start, and does it happen everywhere or only in certain locations?

- Any recent changes (travel, new SIM/eSIM, plan change, software update, new case)?

Quick things to try now:
- Toggle Airplane Mode on for 20 seconds, then off.
- Restart your phone.
- Make sure Cellular Data is on and Network Selection is set to Automatic.
- If you have 5G, try switching to LTE/4G temporarily to see if it stabilizes.
- Toggle Wi‑Fi Calling off/on (if available).
- Check for Carrier Settings and OS updates.
- Reseat the SIM (power off, remove, reinsert). For eSIM, ensure it still shows as active.
- If you’re traveling, enable Data Roaming (if your plan allows).
- Ensure Do Not Disturb/Focus and call forwarding are off; on iPhone, check “Silence Unknown Callers.”
- If you use an MVNO, verify APN settings from your carrier’s support page.

If you want, we can do a quick test:
- Try a test call, send yourself a text, and run a speed test over cellular (not Wi‑Fi).
- Check signal strength: on iPhone, Settings > Cellular > Network Selection (or Field Test mode if available); on Android, Settings > About phone > SIM status. A signal around -50 to -80 dBm is strong; worse than -105 dBm is weak.

Share a bit more about the symptoms and your phone model, and I’ll tailor the next steps.
Uh, yeah, it’s mostly just calls dropping a lot lately. I haven’t really changed anything on my phone, I don’t think.

Thanks for the details. I’m not seeing any outages on our side right now, so let’s zero in on what could cause frequent dropped calls.

A few quick questions to spot the pattern:
- Does it happen mostly in one place (home/office) or everywhere, and is it worse indoors?
- Are you using Wi‑Fi Calling or a Bluetooth headset/car system when it happens?
- What phone model and software version are you on (iPhone/Android)?

Most effective fixes to try now:
- Restart and refresh radios: toggle Airplane Mode on for 20 seconds, then off; then restart the phone.
- Force more stable call mode:
  - iPhone: Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Voice & Data. Select LTE (turn 5G Off/Auto off) and make sure VoLTE is enabled.
  - Android: Settings > Network & Internet (or Connections) > Mobile network > Preferred network type. Choose LTE/4G. Enable VoLTE/Enhanced 4G Calling.
- Wi‑Fi Calling: 
  - If you have strong Wi‑Fi at home/work, turn Wi‑Fi Calling ON and place a test call.
  - If it’s already on and calls drop when you move between Wi‑Fi and cellular, turn it OFF temporarily and test.
- SIM/eSIM check: Power off, remove and reinsert the physical SIM. For eSIM, make sure it still shows as Active; if it looks corrupted, we can walk through re‑adding it.
- Updates and settings:
  - iPhone: Settings > General > About (accept any Carrier Settings update), and install any iOS update.
  - Android: Update OS, and update the Carrier Services app (Google Play). Also ensure Network Selection is set to Automatic.
- Rule out accessories: Try a few calls without Bluetooth/headset and with the case off.
- If issues persist, try Reset Network Settings (this erases saved Wi‑Fi and Bluetooth pairings):
  - iPhone: Settings > General > Transfer or Reset > Reset > Reset Network Settings.
  - Android: Settings > System > Reset options > Reset Wi‑Fi, mobile & Bluetooth.

Quick test to narrow it down:
- Stand near a window or go outdoors and place a 2–3 minute call. If it’s stable there but not indoors, it’s likely a local signal issue. In that case, keeping Wi‑Fi Calling on at home usually fixes it.

If you share your phone model and where it drops (e.g., ZIP or “home near [area]”), I’ll tailor the steps and let you know the best settings to use.
Um, I’m on an iPhone, but I’m not sure which one. It happens mostly at home, I think.

Got it—since it’s mostly at home, this usually points to indoor signal or settings. Let’s try the quickest fixes that stabilize calls on iPhone:

First, two things to try right now
- Turn on Wi‑Fi Calling: Settings > Phone > Wi‑Fi Calling > On, then place a 2–3 minute test call.
- Force a more stable call mode: Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Voice & Data.
  - If you see 5G options, switch to LTE and make sure VoLTE is On.
  - If you don’t see 5G, just make sure VoLTE/Enable LTE is set to Voice & Data.

Then do these quick checks
- Toggle Airplane Mode on for 20 seconds, then off; restart the phone.
- Settings > Cellular > Network Selection > Automatic = On.
- Settings > General > About: accept any Carrier Settings update.
- Settings > General > Software Update: install any iOS update.
- If you use a case with magnets/metal, try a few calls with the case off.
- If you use Bluetooth at home, try a call without it to rule out accessory issues.

If you still see drops
- Try a call near a window or outside. If it’s solid there but not indoors, keep Wi‑Fi Calling on at home.
- Reset Network Settings (this clears saved Wi‑Fi/Bluetooth): Settings > General > Transfer or Reset > Reset > Reset Network Settings.
- If you have a physical SIM: power off, remove and reinsert the SIM. For eSIM: confirm it shows Active in Settings > Cellular.

Helpful to confirm
- Your iPhone model: Settings > General > About > Model Name.
- Do you have strong home Wi‑Fi? If yes, Wi‑Fi Calling should make calls stable.
- Rough area or ZIP (no exact address) where this happens, in case there’s local indoor coverage challenges.

Reply with your iPhone model and whether Wi‑Fi Calling + LTE/VoLTE improved the test call, and I’ll tailor the next steps. If needed, we can also look at options like a network extender, but Wi‑Fi Calling usually fixes at-home drops.
Uh, I think my Wi-Fi is pretty good at home. I haven’t tried that Wi-Fi Calling thing yet though.

Great—since your home Wi‑Fi is solid, Wi‑Fi Calling is the fastest way to stop those drops.

Do this first
- Turn on Wi‑Fi Calling:
  - iPhone: Settings > Phone > Wi‑Fi Calling > turn on “Wi‑Fi Calling on This iPhone.” Follow prompts to confirm your emergency address.
  - If you don’t see this option, tell me—we’ll check carrier settings.
- Quick test to confirm it’s working:
  - Turn on Airplane Mode.
  - Turn Wi‑Fi back on and connect to your home network.
  - Place a 2–3 minute test call. You should see your carrier name with “Wi‑Fi” in the status bar during the call.
  - If the call is stable, turn Airplane Mode off again. Keep Wi‑Fi Calling enabled for everyday use.

If calls still drop after enabling Wi‑Fi Calling
- Force a more stable voice mode:
  - Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Voice & Data > select LTE (turn 5G off) and make sure VoLTE is on.
- Make sure Network Selection is Automatic: Settings > Cellular > Network Selection.
- Accept any Carrier Settings update: Settings > General > About (wait 10–15 seconds for a prompt).
- Restart your iPhone.

Optional Wi‑Fi tune‑up (only if you still see issues)
- Reboot your router.
- If your router offers 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, prefer 5 GHz near the router for best call quality.

Let me know:
- Did the Airplane Mode + Wi‑Fi Calling test call stay connected?
- If not, what happened (failed to start, dropped after X seconds, no audio, etc.)?
- If you don’t see the Wi‑Fi Calling option, which iPhone model is it? You can check under Settings > General > About > Model Name.

You can mostly just flip the switch, but there’s a quick one‑time setup the first time you enable it. Here’s exactly what to do:

Turn it on
- On your iPhone: Settings > Phone > Wi‑Fi Calling.
- Turn on “Wi‑Fi Calling on This iPhone.”
- Follow the prompts to enter/confirm your Emergency (E911) address. This is required so 911 can find you if your phone can’t use GPS/cellular.
- If you get a “Carrier Settings Update” prompt anywhere (often under Settings > General > About), tap Update/Install.

Make sure voice is set to a stable mode
- Go to Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Voice & Data.
- If you see 5G options, pick LTE for now and make sure VoLTE is On. You can switch back later if things are stable.
- If you only see LTE, ensure it’s set to Voice & Data.

Quick test to confirm it’s working
- Turn on Airplane Mode.
- Turn Wi‑Fi back on and connect to your home Wi‑Fi.
- Place a 2–3 minute call (voicemail is fine). You should see “Wi‑Fi” next to your carrier name during the call.
- If it’s solid, turn Airplane Mode off again and leave Wi‑Fi Calling on for everyday use.

If the option is missing or won’t stay on
- Update iOS (Settings > General > Software Update) and accept any Carrier Settings update (Settings > General > About).
- Restart the iPhone.
- Make sure Network Selection is set to Automatic (Settings > Cellular).
- If you use a VPN on the phone or your router, turn it off and try again—some VPNs block Wi‑Fi Calling.
- If it still doesn’t appear, your plan or carrier settings may need Wi‑Fi Calling enabled on their side—tell me your carrier and iPhone model, and I’ll guide you, or you can contact the carrier to enable it.

If calls still drop on Wi‑Fi

Want me to stay on the line while you try the Airplane Mode test? If you run into any prompt or error, tell me what you see and your iPhone model (Settings > General > About > Model Name), and I’ll adjust the steps.
Okay, I’ll give it a shot in a bit. If I get stuck or something weird pops up, I’ll let you know.

Sounds good—take your time. Quick reminders for when you try:
- Turn on Wi‑Fi Calling: Settings > Phone > Wi‑Fi Calling, confirm the emergency address.

If anything is missing or errors pop up, tell me:

- Exactly what you see (missing toggle, greyed out, error message).

If the toggle is missing/greyed out, try: update iOS, accept any Carrier Settings update (Settings > General > About), ensure Network Selection is Automatic, turn off any VPN, then restart.

I’m here whenever you’re ready.
Alright, cool. I’ll mess with it when I get a chance. If it’s still acting up or I can’t figure it out, I’ll come back here. Thanks.

You’re welcome! Wi‑Fi Calling usually clears up at‑home drops, so hopefully that does it.

If it’s still acting up, just come back with:

Hmm, I mean, I guess it’s online, but sometimes stuff just doesn’t load right. Not sure if it’s my wifi or something else.

Intermittent “pages not loading” can come from a few different places: weak/unstable Wi‑Fi link, DNS hiccups, ISP congestion, or a problem with a specific site/app. Here’s a quick way to narrow it down and some fixes you can try now.

Quick isolation checklist
- Check scope: Does it happen on all sites/apps or just some? Does another device on the same Wi‑Fi see the same slowdown at the same time? If only one device/app is affected, it’s likely device/app‑specific.
- Try a wired test (if possible): Plug a computer into the router with Ethernet. If wired is smooth while Wi‑Fi isn’t, it’s a Wi‑Fi issue (signal/interference/band steering). If wired also struggles, it’s likely ISP or modem/router.
- Run three quick connectivity checks when the issue happens:
  1) Ping your router/gateway (often 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1). If you see loss or big spikes here, it’s the local Wi‑Fi link.
  2) Ping 8.8.8.8 (Google DNS). If router ping is fine but this shows loss/latency spikes, it’s your ISP/connection beyond the router.
  3) Ping google.com. If 1 and 2 are fine but this fails, it’s likely DNS.
  If you want, tell me your device/OS and I’ll give exact steps.
- Do a quick speed test and note latency/jitter and whether upload is saturated. If upload is pegged (cloud backups, video calls), everything can feel slow.

Easy fixes to try
- Wi‑Fi link quality:
  - Move closer to the router and see if it stabilizes.
  - Try the other band: 5 GHz is faster but shorter range; 2.4 GHz goes farther but is crowded. If your router has “Smart Connect,” try temporarily splitting SSIDs so you can pick 2.4 vs 5 GHz explicitly.
  - Change the Wi‑Fi channel (especially on 2.4 GHz). Neighbors’ networks and devices like microwaves/Bluetooth can cause interference.
- DNS:
  - Temporarily set DNS to 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8 on your device or router to rule out DNS issues.
- Device/app specifics:
  - Disable VPN/proxy for a bit and retest.
  - Clear browser/app cache; try another browser.
  - Forget the Wi‑Fi network and rejoin it; renew DHCP lease.
- Router/modem:
  - Reboot the router and modem.
  - Update router firmware.
  - Ensure the router isn’t overheating and is placed in the open, centrally.
  - If your router has QoS/SQM, enable it to reduce bufferbloat during uploads.

If you can share a bit more, I can pinpoint it faster:
- Does it affect all sites/apps or only some? Any error messages?
- Do other devices on the same Wi‑Fi have the issue at the same time?
- Can you try a quick wired test?
- Your device/OS and router model? Any VPN in use?
- Roughly how far are you from the router and how many walls in between?

Give me the results of the ping checks or speed test, and I’ll suggest the next exact step.

Got it. Since it’s only on your laptop and you’re one room away, it could be a Wi‑Fi signal blip, DNS hiccup, or something on the laptop (VPN, background upload). Here’s a quick 2–3 minute check to pinpoint it:

Do these when the “stuck loading” happens
- Try another device: Grab your phone on the same Wi‑Fi and load the same site at the same time. 
  - If the phone is fine while the laptop hangs, it’s likely laptop-specific.
  - If both hang, it’s likely Wi‑Fi/ISP/DNS.

- Run three pings from your laptop:
  1) Ping your router (gateway). If this shows loss or big spikes, it’s the local Wi‑Fi link.
  2) Ping 1.1.1.1 (internet without DNS). If router ping is fine but this is bad, it’s your ISP/connection beyond the router.
  3) Ping google.com (adds DNS). If 1 and 2 are fine but this fails, it’s likely DNS.
  Windows:
    - Find gateway: ipconfig | findstr /i "Default Gateway"
    - Then: ping -n 20 GATEWAY_IP
            ping -n 20 1.1.1.1
            ping -n 20 google.com
  macOS:
    - Find gateway: netstat -nr | grep default
    - Then: ping -c 20 GATEWAY_IP
            ping -c 20 1.1.1.1
            ping -c 20 google.com

- Quick speed test: Run a test (e.g., speedtest.net) and note ping/jitter and whether upload is maxed out.

Fast fixes to try now

- Try the other band: If you can see both “YourWiFi” and “YourWiFi‑5G/5GHz,” switch bands. 5 GHz is faster but doesn’t go through walls as well; 2.4 GHz goes farther but is crowded.

2) Ping the internet without DNS:

3) Ping using DNS:
  ping -n 20 google.com
